title: Fetal growth restriction: SGA vs FGR, Doppler velocimetry, biophysical profile and delivery timing
subject: ss-obg
refs: Williams Obstetrics 25e Ch 17 (Fetal Assessment), Ch 44 (Fetal-Growth Disorders)
SMFM Consult Series #52: Diagnosis and management of fetal growth restriction
ISUOG Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis and management of small-for-gestational-age fetus

steps.say: Distinguishing between constitutionally small fetuses and true pathological growth restriction is vital to prevent unnecessary iatrogenic prematurity. Small for gestational age describes an estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile, whereas fetal growth restriction denotes pathological failure to attain genetic growth potential accompanied by abnormal Doppler flow.
steps.tx: Perinatal definitions distinguish **small for gestational age** (constitutionally small fetus with **estimated fetal weight** < 10th percentile and normal hemodynamics) from true pathological **fetal growth restriction**, which reflects chronic placental insufficiency, abnormal **Doppler velocimetry**, oligohydramnios, or weight dropping below the severe 3rd percentile.

vis.caption: Sequential Doppler velocimetry deterioration in placental vascular insufficiency. Credit: StewardMD.
vis.alt: Doppler waveform progression from increased resistance to absent and reversed end-diastolic flow.

steps.say: Pathological growth restriction exhibits distinct morphological patterns based on the timing and mechanism of insult. Symmetric growth restriction presents with proportionate reduction of head, abdomen, and long bones from early first-trimester genetic or infectious insults, while asymmetric restriction exhibits head-sparing brain preservation from late uteroplacental compromise.
steps.tx: Early-onset **symmetric FGR** presents with proportional head and abdominal circumference reductions from early aneuploidy, structural malformations, or congenital TORCH infection, whereas late-onset **asymmetric FGR** demonstrates **head-sparing** redistribution with preserved head circumference and wasted abdominal girth caused by chronic **uteroplacental insufficiency**.

left.title: Symmetric Growth Restriction (20-30%)
points: Proportionate reduction: HC, BPD, AC, and FL all < 10th centile
Early onset: genetic aneuploidies, viral TORCH infections
Total cellular hypoplasia; normal Doppler velocimetry

right.title: Asymmetric Growth Restriction (70-80%)
points: Disproportionate: AC small, HC and FL relatively spared
Late onset: maternal vascular disease, preeclampsia
Cellular hypertrophy preserved; abnormal umbilical Doppler

steps.say: Umbilical artery Doppler velocimetry provides direct hemodynamic insight into downstream placental tertiary villous vascular resistance. As vascular obliteration advances beyond 60 to 70 percent of villi, diastolic velocity progressively drops, culminating in absent end-diastolic flow and ominous reversed end-diastolic flow.
steps.tx: Evaluation of **umbilical artery Doppler** monitors placental resistance; progressive villous vascular obliteration reduces diastolic forward flow, progressing from high resistance to complete **absent end-diastolic flow** (AEDF) and finally dangerous **reversed end-diastolic flow** (REDF), signaling severe impending fetal acidemia and intrauterine demise.

nodes.label: Normal umbilical artery waveform: high diastolic velocity with low S/D ratio
Early placental disease: elevated pulsatility index with reduced end-diastolic flow
Severe villous damage: absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF)
Critical late deterioration: reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF)

steps.say: When placental resistance surges, the compromised fetus initiates an adaptive hemodynamic redistribution. The middle cerebral artery undergoes active vasodilation to protect perfusion of the cerebral cortex, resulting in a marked drop in middle cerebral artery pulsatility index below the fifth percentile.
steps.tx: In response to progressive hypoxia, the fetus mounts an adaptive circulatory redistribution termed **brain-sparing effect**, causing cerebral vasodilation that lowers the **middle cerebral artery** pulsatility index below the 5th percentile and elevates the **cerebroplacental ratio** (CPR) to abnormal values, predicting adverse perinatal outcomes.

rows: Elevated PI, progress to AEDF or REDF
Abnormal CPR < 1.08 (highly sensitive for adverse outcome)
Absent or reversed a-wave during atrial systole

steps.say: Ductus venosus Doppler velocimetry serves as the ultimate hemodynamic barometer of fetal myocardial acidemia. The appearance of an absent or reversed a-wave during atrial contraction indicates severe right ventricular afterload and impending intrauterine demise within 24 to 48 hours.
steps.tx: The **ductus venosus** waveform reflects right ventricular cardiac function; disappearance or reversal of forward flow during the **reversed a-wave** (atrial systole) indicates advanced myocardial strain, profound metabolic acidemia, and imminent **fetal demise**, providing the primary objective hemodynamic trigger for delivery before 32 weeks.

nodes.label: Assess ductus venosus triphasic waveform (S, D, and a waves)
Identify loss of forward flow or negative deflection of a-wave
Confirms advanced myocardial decompensation and acidemia
Trigger emergency delivery after immediate steroid coverage

steps.say: The biophysical profile combines acute and chronic markers of central nervous system oxygenation. Manning's score evaluates fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone, amniotic fluid volume, and the reactive non-stress test, yielding a maximum score of 10 points.
steps.tx: The **Manning biophysical profile** scores 5 parameters (each scored 0 or 2): **fetal breathing movements** (>= 30 sec), gross body movements (>= 3), **fetal tone** (>= 1 active extension/flexion), amniotic fluid (pocket >= 2 cm), and non-stress test, where scores <= 4 mandate prompt delivery.

rows: >= 1 episode of active extension and flexion
Slow extension or absent active flexion

steps.say: Cardiotocographic fetal monitoring requires mature neurocardiac autonomic integration. In pregnancies at or beyond 32 weeks gestation, a reactive non-stress test requires at least two accelerations rising 15 beats per minute above baseline and lasting 15 seconds within a 20-minute window.
steps.tx: In gestations at or beyond 32 weeks, a **reactive non-stress test** demonstrates autonomic stability by showing at least 2 distinct **accelerations** peaking >= 15 bpm above baseline and lasting >= 15 seconds (**15x15 rule**) within a standard 20-minute recording interval, reflecting healthy brainstem and cardiovascular oxygenation.

left.title: Reactive NST Criteria (>= 32 weeks)
points: Two or more accelerations in 20 minutes
Peak >= 15 bpm above baseline, lasting >= 15 sec
Indicates healthy fetal autonomic and brainstem oxygenation

right.title: Preterm Criteria (< 32 weeks)
points: Lower acceleration threshold avoids misclassifying healthy preterm fetuses

steps.say: Determining the timing of delivery balances the risk of intrauterine stillbirth against the morbidity of extreme neonatal prematurity. Obstetric guidelines mandate delivery at 32 weeks for persistent reversed end-diastolic flow, and at 34 weeks for absent end-diastolic flow following antenatal corticosteroid administration.
steps.tx: Clinical guidelines for **delivery timing** in FGR balance prematurity against stillbirth: **umbilical artery Doppler** with reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF) mandates delivery at 32 weeks, absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) triggers delivery at 34 weeks, and uncomplicated FGR with normal Dopplers delivers at 37 weeks under **steroid coverage**.
